questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081888/assets/9542a7ddac8932b40e6f3a4217e7d97af6d1f3fc2598c595f9661ef5bc2b98ee.png)

The total area $A$ of the region between the curve $y=\frac{12}{{x}^{2}+2}-2$ and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=3$ is given by the following integral expression below: 

$$
A={\int }_{1}^{a}(\frac{12}{{x}^{2}+2}-2)\text{d}x\,-{\int }_{a}^{3}(\frac{12}{{x}^{2}+2}-2)\text{d}x
$$

Find the value of $a.$ Do not round the answer.

$a=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To determine the missing limit of integration, we need to find the $x$-intercept of the curve $y=\frac{12}{{x}^{2}+2}-2.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{12}{{x}^{2}+2}-2 & =0 \\ \frac{12}{{x}^{2}+2} & =2 \\ 12 & =2({x}^{2}+2) \\ 12 & =2{x}^{2}+4 \\ 8 & =2{x}^{2} \\ 4 & ={x}^{2} \\ \pm 2 & =x \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution between $x=1$ and $x=3$ is $x=2.$

Since $2\in [1,3],$ we have two regions:

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=2.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=2$ to $x=3.$

So, $a=2$ and the final expression will be

$$
A={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{12}{{x}^{2}+2}-2)\text{d}x\,-\,{\int }_{2}^{3}(\frac{12}{{x}^{2}+2}-2)\text{d}x.
$$

The total area $A$ of the region between the curve $y=\frac{1}{16}(x+2)^{4}-1$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-5$ to $x=-1$ is given by the integral expression below. What is the value of $a?$

$$
A={\int }_{-5}^{a}(\frac{1}{16}(x+2)^{4}-1)\text{d}x-{\int }_{a}^{-1}(\frac{1}{16}(x+2)^{4}-1)\text{d}x.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine the missing limit of integration, we need to find the $x$-intercept of the curve $y=\frac{1}{16}(x+2)^{4}-1.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16}(x+2)^{4}-1 & =0 \\ \frac{1}{16}(x+2)^{4} & =1 \\ (x+2)^{4} & =16 \\ \sqrt[4]{(x+2)^{4}} & =\pm \sqrt[4]{16} \\ x+2 & =\pm \sqrt[4]{{2}^{4}} \\ x+2 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =-4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution between $x=-5$ and $x=-1$ is $x=-4.$

Since $-4\in [-5,-1],$ we have two regions:

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-5$ to $x=-4.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-4$ to $x=-1.$

So, $a=-4$ and the final expression will be

$$
A={\int }_{-5}^{-4}(\frac{1}{16}(x+2)^{4}-1)\text{d}x-{\int }_{-4}^{-1}(\frac{1}{16}(x+2)^{4}-1)\text{d}x.
$$

$$
A=-{\int }_{-2}^{a}(1-\frac{4}{x+3})\text{d}x+{\int }_{a}^{5}(1-\frac{4}{x+3})\text{d}x.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine the missing limit of integration, we need to find the $x$-intercept of the curve $y=1-\frac{4}{x+3}.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{4}{x+3} & =0 \\ -\frac{4}{x+3} & =-1 \\ \frac{4}{x+3} & =1 \\ 4 & =x+3 \\ 1 & =x \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since $1\in [-2,5],$ we have two regions:

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=1.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=5.$

So, $a=1$ and the final expression will be

$$
A=-{\int }_{-2}^{1}(1-\frac{4}{x+3})\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{5}(1-\frac{4}{x+3})\text{d}x.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-2{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(3-2x) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=\frac{3}{2}.$

So, $a=\frac{3}{2}$ and the final expression will be

A={\int }_{1}^{3/2}(3x-2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{3/2}^{\sqrt{10}}(3x-2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.

The total area $A$ of the region between the curve $y=\frac{1}{9}(x-1)^{4}-1$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=0$ is given by the following integral expression below: 

$$
A={\int }_{-2}^{a}(\frac{1}{9}(x-1)^{4}-1)\text{d}x\,-\,{\int }_{a}^{0}(\frac{1}{9}(x-1)^{4}-1)\text{d}x
$$

Find the value of $a.$ Do not round the answer.

$a=$
{{field-1}}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{9}(x-1)^{4}-1 & =0 \\ \frac{1}{9}(x-1)^{4} & =1 \\ (x-1)^{4} & =9 \\ \sqrt[4]{(x-1)^{4}} & =\pm \sqrt[4]{9} \\ x-1 & =\pm {9}^{1/4}\,=\,\pm \sqrt{3} \\ x & =1\pm \sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution between $x=-2$ and $x=0$ is $x=1-\sqrt{3}.$

Since $1-\sqrt{3}\in [-2,0],$ we have two regions:

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=1-\sqrt{3}.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1-\sqrt{3}$ to $x=0.$

So, $a=1-\sqrt{3}$ and the final expression will be

$$
A={\int }_{-2}^{1-\sqrt{3}}(\frac{1}{9}(x-1)^{4}-1)\text{d}x\,-\,{\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{0}(\frac{1}{9}(x-1)^{4}-1)\text{d}x.
$$

questions.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=4{x}^{3}+4$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}+4 & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =-1 \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-1$ is our only real solution. Since $-1\in [-2,1]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=-1.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081888/assets/b0f2899bf6a946f6d7bf8bc60c41827bd05aef500f0fc0f30a5916c26b1007bb.png)

Notice that the region for $x\in [-2,-1]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{-1}(4{x}^{3}+4)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{-2}^{-1}(4{x}^{3}+4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4{\int }_{-2}^{-1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x-4{\int }_{-2}^{-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{x}^{4}{|}_{-2}^{-1}-4x{|}_{-2}^{-1} \\  & =-[(-1)^{4}-(-2)^{4}]-4[-1+2] \\  & =-(-15)-4 \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [-1,1]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(4{x}^{3}+4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+4{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{4}{|}_{-1}^{1}+4x{|}_{-1}^{-1} \\  & =[{1}^{4}-(-1)^{4}]+4[1-(-1)] \\  & =0+8 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=11+8=19.
$$

questions.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=3{x}^{3}+24$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{3}+24 & =0 \\ 3{x}^{3} & =-24 \\ {x}^{3} & =-8 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-2\in [-3,-1]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=-2.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=-1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081888/assets/80315b4862adf8ebb1f91f5c4c7606a59dfa5738c40e34179a745e03a0a25693.png)

Notice that the region for $x\in [-3,-2]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-3}^{-2}(3{x}^{3}+24)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{-3}^{-2}(3{x}^{3}+24)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3{\int }_{-3}^{-2}({x}^{3}+8)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3\cdot {(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+8x)|}_{-3}^{-2} \\  & =-3\cdot ([4-16]-[\frac{81}{4}-24]) \\  & =-3\cdot (-12+\frac{15}{4}) \\  & =-3\cdot (-\frac{33}{4}) \\  & =\frac{99}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [-2,-1],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{-1}(3{x}^{3}+24)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{-2}^{-1}({x}^{3}+8)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\cdot {(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+8x)|}_{-2}^{-1} \\  & =3\cdot ([\frac{1}{4}-8]-[4-16]) \\  & =3\cdot (-\frac{31}{4}+12) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{17}{4} \\  & =\frac{51}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{99}{4}+\frac{51}{4}=\frac{75}{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081888/assets/47e15993f3957fb3c1d7619fcf62544b2d5b358715538e17b9232dec5a0172c7.png)

Find the total area of the region between the curve $y={x}^{4}-1$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=2$, as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{4}-1 & =0 \\ {x}^{4} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution between $x=0$ and $x=2$ is $x=1.$

Since $1\in [0,2]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=2.$

Notice that the region for $x\in [0,1]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}-x)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-[\frac{1}{5}-1]-0 \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [1,2]$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}-x)|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =([\frac{32}{5}-2]-[\frac{1}{5}-1]) \\  & =\frac{26}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{4}{5}+\frac{26}{5}=\frac{30}{5}=6.
$$

questions.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=3x-{x}^{2}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(3-x) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $3\in [1,4],$ we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=3.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=3$ to $x=4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081888/assets/219d7aa5b976c97d47a96d0c94c3d61d139d5ddddc55b82d0df68f19ad6d5149.png)

Notice that the region for $x\in [3,4]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{3}^{4}(3x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(3x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{3}x\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{1}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}\,{|}_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}\,{|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[{3}^{2}-{1}^{2}]-\frac{1}{3}[{3}^{3}-{1}^{3}] \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[9-1]-\frac{1}{3}[27-1] \\  & =12-\frac{26}{3} \\  & =\frac{10}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [3,4],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =-{\int }_{3}^{4}(3x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3{\int }_{3}^{4}x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}\,{|}_{3}^{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}\,{|}_{3}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}[{4}^{2}-{3}^{2}]+\frac{1}{3}[{4}^{3}-{3}^{3}] \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}[16-9]+\frac{1}{3}[64-27] \\  & =-\frac{21}{2}+\frac{37}{3} \\  & =\frac{11}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{10}{3}+\frac{11}{6}=\frac{31}{6}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081888/assets/fc09b3b302a0920562a3ca03f52a2f6f98dc327b89f231e07b8a6ab631a48b2b.png)

Find the total area $A$ of the region between the curve $y={x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=4,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}(x-3) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $3\in [1,4],$ we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=3.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=3$ to $x=4.$

Notice that the region for $x\in [1,3]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{3}({x}^{3}-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{1}^{3}({x}^{3}-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{1}^{3}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+3{\int }_{1}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}\,{|}_{1}^{3}+{x}^{3}\,{|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}[{3}^{4}-{1}^{4}]+[{3}^{3}-{1}^{3}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}[81-1]+[27-1] \\  & =-20+26 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [3,4],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{3}^{4}({x}^{3}-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}\,{|}_{3}^{4}-{x}^{3}\,{|}_{3}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[{4}^{4}-{3}^{4}]-[{4}^{3}-{3}^{3}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[256-81]-[64-27] \\  & =\frac{175}{4}-37 \\  & =\frac{27}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={A}_{1}+{A}_{2} \\  & =6+\frac{27}{4} \\  & =\frac{24}{4}+\frac{27}{4} \\  & =\frac{51}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081888/assets/a4871287696f20009bd7d2b8793965c9f68e35faa4ad150477643f1d3ec77e38.png)

Which integral expression gives the total area enclosed between the curve $y={x}^{5}-{x}^{4}-6{x}^{3}$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the limits of integration. We find the $x$-intercepts of the curve as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5}-{x}^{4}-6{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{3}({x}^{2}-x-6) & =0 \\ {x}^{3}(x+2)(x-3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $x=-2,x=0$ or $x=3.$ Since $0\in [-2,3],$ we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=3.$

For $x\in [-2,0]$, we have

$$
{A}_{1}={\int }_{-2}^{0}({x}^{5}-{x}^{4}-6{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that for $x\in [0,3]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{5}-{x}^{4}-6{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
{A}_{2}=-{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{5}-{x}^{4}-6{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{3}-({x}^{5}-{x}^{4}-6{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x.
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}={\int }_{-2}^{0}({x}^{5}-{x}^{4}-6{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{3}-({x}^{5}-{x}^{4}-6{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x.
$$

questions.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=27-3{x}^{2}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=5.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}27-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2} & =27 \\ {x}^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-3$ and $x=3$ are our real solutions. Since $3\in [-3,5]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=3.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=3$ to $x=5.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081888/assets/6b3ca7be487585b296aaeb0b3fa7eb4ce8b9b4f9ad35d52baefa04f2fbbed621.png)

For $x\in [-3,3]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{3}(27-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =27{\int }_{-3}^{3}\,\text{d}x-3{\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =27x{|}_{-3}^{3}-{x}^{3}{|}_{-3}^{3} \\  & =27[3-(-3)]-[(3)^{3}-(-3)^{3}] \\  & =162-54 \\  & =108.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for $x\in [3,5]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{3}^{5}(27-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =-{\int }_{3}^{5}(27-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-27{\int }_{3}^{5}\,\text{d}x+3{\int }_{3}^{5}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-27x{|}_{3}^{5}+{x}^{3}{|}_{3}^{5} \\  & =-27[5-3]+[(5)^{3}-(3)^{3}] \\  & =-54+98 \\  & =44.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=108+44=152.
$$

Which integral expression gives the total area enclosed between the curve $y=9{x}^{3}-{x}^{5}$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the limits of integration. We find the $x$-intercepts of the curve as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{3}-{x}^{5} & =0 \\ {x}^{3}(9-{x}^{2}) & =0 \\ {x}^{3}(3-x)(3+x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $x=\pm 3$ or $x=0.$ Since $0\in [-3,3],$ we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=3.$

Notice that for $x\in [-3,0]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-3}^{0}(9{x}^{3}-{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
{A}_{2}=-{\int }_{-3}^{0}(9{x}^{3}-{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-3}^{0}-(9{x}^{3}-{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x.
$$

For $x\in [0,3]$, we have

$$
{A}_{2}={\int }_{0}^{3}(9{x}^{3}-{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x.
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}={\int }_{-3}^{0}-(9{x}^{3}-{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{3}(9{x}^{3}-{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The total area $A$ of the region between the curve $y=x^3-1$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=2$ is given by the integral expression below. What is the value of $a?$

$$
A = \displaystyle -\int_{-2}^{a} (x^3-1) \:\textrm{d}x + \int_{a}^{2} (x^3-1) \:\textrm{d}x
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081888/assets/57d01ea60e3cd9770f2ef978e46e2cef7b69a9fcdc2ac478d5b6c73d8f366c7b.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To determine the missing limit of integration, we need to find the $x$-intercept of the curve $y=x^3-1.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={x}^{3}-1 \\ (0) & ={x}^{3}-1 \\ {x}^{3} & =1 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $1 \in [-2,2]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x={\color{blue}{1}}.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x={\color{blue}{1}}$ to $x=2.$

So, $a={\color{blue}1}$ and the final expression will be

$$
A = \displaystyle -\int_{-2}^{\color{blue}1} (x^3-1) \:\textrm{d}x + \int_{\color{blue}1}^{2} (x^3-1) \:\textrm{d}x.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x^3$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=\dfrac{3}{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081888/assets/0d3ede3cfbec765228ea184c74e0cb35f1df2a9340bd1cb703a0990249fecf30.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $0 \in \left[-1,\dfrac{3}{2}\right]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{3}{2}.$

Notice that for $x \in  [-1,0]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
\int_{a}^{b} y(x) \:\textrm{d}x = \int_{-1}^{0}  \dfrac{x^3}{2}  \:\textrm{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
A_1 = -\int_{-1}^{0}  \dfrac{x^3}{2}  \:\textrm{d}x .
$$

For $x \in\left[0,\dfrac{3}{2}\right]$, we have

$$
A_2 = \int_{0}^{3/2}\dfrac{x^3}{2} \:\textrm{d}x.
$$

The total area is

$$
A = A_1+A_2 = - \int_{-1}^{0} \dfrac{x^3}{2}  \:\textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{3/2} \dfrac{x^3}{2}  \:\textrm{d}x .
$$

 

Finally, we carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =-{\int }_{-1}^{0}\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{3/2}\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{8}]}_{-1}^{0}+{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{8}]}_{0}^{3/2} \\  & =-[0-\frac{1}{8}]+[\frac{81}{128}-0] \\  & =\frac{1}{8}+\frac{81}{128} \\  & =\frac{97}{128}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=x^3-9x$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-9x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-9) & =0 \\ x(x-3)(x+3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=0,$ $x=-3,$ and $x=3$ are our real solutions. Since $0 \in [-3,3]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081888/assets/29a51c9892de59037e84bace2f8b5822222c3056a05af861cbd741390a437a61.png)

For $x \in [-3,0]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{0}({x}^{3}-9x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{0}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x-9{\int }_{-3}^{0}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}{|}_{-3}^{0}-\frac{9{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{-3}^{0} \\  & =[0-\frac{(-3)^{4}}{4}]-9[0-\frac{(-3)^{2}}{2}] \\  & =-\frac{81}{4}+\frac{81}{2} \\  & =\frac{81}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for $x \in [0,3]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
\int_{a}^{b} y(x) \:\textrm{d}x = \int_{0}^{3} \left(x^3-9x\right) \:\textrm{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{3}-9x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+9{\int }_{0}^{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}{|}_{0}^{3}+\frac{9{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-[\frac{(3)^{4}}{4}-0]+9[\frac{(3)^{2}}{2}-0] \\  & =-\frac{81}{4}+\frac{81}{2} \\  & =\frac{81}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A = A_1+A_2 =  \dfrac{81}{4} + \dfrac{81}{4} = \dfrac{81}{2}.
$$
